result: CL assembles into polymers in solution with an 8-mer as the basic structural unit. Multiple biophysical techniques (SDS-PAGE, IM-MS, analytical ultracentrifugation, mass photometry, TEM, AFM) demonstrate that CL forms oligomers and larger assemblies in solution, with evidence supporting an 8-mer as the fundamental building block that polymerizes into linear structures and loops.
evaluation: Claims C3, C31-C54 are supported by convergent evidence from multiple independent techniques (IM-MS, mass photometry, analytical ultracentrifugation, TEM, AFM). The 8-mer assignment is based on collisional cross-section agreement between experimental (2567 Ų) and theoretical (2500 Ų) values (C37), AFM height and volume analysis (C50-C53), and modeling. The authors acknowledge uncertainty in the precise stoichiometry (C130-C131), which is appropriate given the technical challenges.

result: CL polymers grow by sequential head-to-toe addition of 8-mer subunits. AFM volume analysis shows stepwise increases consistent with sequential addition of subunits (C49), and modeling of head-to-toe assemblies agrees with experimental volumes (C56). Loops in solution are proposed to contain approximately six head-to-toe 8-mers (C81).
evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C55-C57, C80-C81 are supported by AFM volume analysis showing stepwise growth (C49) and agreement between simulated and experimental volumes for head-to-toe arrangements (C56). The head-to-toe model is further validated by mutational analysis (G4W affecting N-terminus) and is consistent across multiple lines of evidence.

result: CL forms two distinct types of membrane pores: unrimmed pores (simple depressions) and rimmed pores (surrounded by discrete protrusions ~0.3 nm above the bilayer). AFM imaging reveals that unrimmed pores are dynamic and have a broad area distribution (41 nm²), while rimmed pores are more stable with a narrower distribution (26 nm²). Both pore types diffuse freely in the bilayer.
evaluation: Claims C58-C69 and C11 are well-supported by AFM imaging data showing two morphologically distinct pore types with different area distributions, stability profiles, and dynamic behavior. Time-series AFM imaging (C67-C68) provides direct evidence for the differential stability. The observation that both pore types diffuse (C62) rules out artifacts from surface interactions.

result: CL loops formed in solution spontaneously insert into membranes to become unrimmed pores. The similarity in size and shape between solution loops and unrimmed pores (C70), combined with direct observation of loops at sites where pores existed after lipid dissociation (C72), supports this mechanism. Detergent removal experiments confirm that loops remain after lipid is removed (C76-C77).
evaluation: Claims C6, C70-C77, C115 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: (1) area distribution similarity between loops and unrimmed pores (C70), (2) direct AFM observation of loops at former pore sites after spontaneous lipid dissociation (C72), and (3) controlled detergent removal experiments (C75-C77). The inference that loops become pores is well-justified by the convergent data.

result: Rimmed pores form through a maturation mechanism involving 90-degree rotation of 8-mer subunits from head-to-toe to side-by-side orientation. OCD data indicate predominant transmembrane helix orientation consistent with rimmed pores, with a population of membrane-parallel helices consistent with unrimmed pores (C84-C86). The rim height (~0.3 nm) corresponds to helix ends protruding from the bilayer (C121).
evaluation: Claims C12-C13, C79, C84-C86, C121-C123, C135-C137 propose a maturation mechanism based on modeling and OCD data. While the OCD data support mixed helix orientations (C84-C86) and AFM shows rimmed pores are more stable (C68), the 90-degree rotation mechanism is largely inferred from modeling rather than directly observed. The progressive maturation (C122) is suggested but not rigorously quantified. Additional structural data would strengthen this conclusion.

result: The G4W mutation prevents CL polymerization in solution and abolishes pore formation and cellular toxicity. Mass photometry and AFM show G4W forms few large assemblies (C90, C93), no membrane pores are observed by AFM (C95), liposome dye release assays show no membrane disruption (C96), and epithelial cells show no danger response activation (C9). This demonstrates that polymerization in solution is necessary for membrane damage.
evaluation: Claims C7-C10, C90, C93, C95-C96, C102, C104 are strongly supported by convergent loss-of-function data across multiple assays (mass photometry, AFM, liposome leakage, Western blot). The G4W mutation provides a critical test of the polymerization-dependent mechanism. The conclusion that polymerization is necessary for membrane damage (C10, C104) is well-justified by the complete loss of function across all assays.

result: The I9A variant shows enhanced polymerization, increased loop formation, larger membrane pores, and greater membrane disruption compared to wild-type CL. Mass photometry shows efficient self-assembly (C91), AFM reveals increased loop features (C92) and larger pores (C133-C134), liposome assays show enhanced membrane disruption (C98), and cellular assays show significantly higher c-Fos expression (C108).
evaluation: Claims C91-C92, C94, C97-C98, C100-C101, C108, C133-C134 are supported by consistent gain-of-function data across biophysical and cellular assays. The correlation between increased loop formation in solution (C92) and larger pores in membranes (C133-C134) provides strong support for the loop-to-pore mechanism. SDS-PAGE data showing higher oligomer levels (C100-C101) provides a mechanistic explanation.

result: CL forms α-helical structure in solution, with modest additional helix formation in the presence of lipid vesicles. CD spectroscopy shows characteristic α-helix minima at 208 and 222 nm (C82). The G4W variant shows reduced helical structure in both solution and lipid environments (C99).
evaluation: Claims C82-C83, C99 are supported by CD spectroscopy data. The α-helical structure in solution (C82) is consistent with prior literature (Moyes et al., 2016) and the 8-mer coiled-coil model. The reduced helicity of G4W (C99) may contribute to its loss of function, though the relative importance of structural versus assembly defects is unclear.

result: CL-induced membrane damage activates danger response signaling in epithelial cells, with mutations affecting polymerization impacting cellular responses. Wild-type CL induces robust c-Fos expression (3-fold) and MKP1 phosphorylation (5-fold) in TR146 cells (C107), while mutations that alter polymerization (I9A, G4W) show corresponding changes in cellular signaling (C109).
evaluation: Claims C105-C107, C109-C110 are supported by Western blot data showing differential activation of danger response markers (c-Fos, pMKP1) by CL variants. The correlation between polymerization ability and cellular response (C109-C110) is consistent across the three variants tested, though the sample size (N=4) is modest. The conclusion that polymerization is a major factor in infection (C110) is well-supported.

result: CL uses a novel pore formation mechanism distinct from typical pore-forming toxins, involving pre-assembly of loops in solution that insert into membranes. This represents a previously unknown mechanism for membrane pore formation and identifies CL polymerization as a therapeutic target.
evaluation: Claims C14, C113-C114, C132 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by the totality of evidence showing: (1) polymerization in solution (multiple techniques), (2) loop formation before membrane binding (AFM), (3) loop insertion to form pores (detergent removal, area similarity), and (4) necessity of polymerization for function (G4W mutation). The novelty claim is justified by comparison with known PFT mechanisms (C111-C112).

result: CL forms intermediate-sized membrane pores (~80 Å diameter) that are smaller than pores formed by gasdermin-D, suilysin, and perfringolysin O, but likely larger than α-hemolysin pores. Unrimmed CL pores are topographically similar to melittin-induced structures, while rimmed pores are more stable on AFM imaging timescales.
evaluation: Claims C116-C120 are supported by AFM area measurements and comparisons with literature values for other pore-forming proteins. The pore size calculation from area distributions (C116) is reasonable assuming circularity. The comparison with melittin (C119) is appropriate given the similar topography, though functional similarities are not established.

result: Linear CL polymers can insert into membranes without causing visible membrane disruption, but become pores when they close into loops. This is inferred from AFM observations after lipid removal showing linear features that were previously obscured by the bilayer.
evaluation: Claims C126 and C73 are supported by AFM observations after spontaneous or detergent-induced lipid dissociation showing linear polymers that were not visible when the bilayer was intact. This suggests linear polymers insert but don't disrupt the bilayer surface significantly. The inference is reasonable but relies on the assumption that the structures observed after lipid removal reflect the pre-removal state.

result: The stability difference between unrimmed and rimmed pores may relate to lysine residue positioning. In unrimmed pores, lysine side chains would contact lipids (meta-stable), while in rimmed pores they would be solvent-exposed (more stable).
evaluation: Claims C124-C125 are speculative proposals about the energetic basis for pore maturation. While the reasoning about charged residue positioning is plausible, there is no direct experimental evidence (e.g., mutagenesis of lysine residues, molecular dynamics simulations) to support this specific mechanism. The speculation is reasonable but requires validation.

result: The pre-assembly mechanism may provide an infectivity advantage for C. albicans and represents a therapeutic opportunity. Molecules that prevent CL polymerization or loop formation could serve as therapeutics against C. albicans infection.
evaluation: Claims C127-C129 are speculative proposals about biological significance and therapeutic potential. While the logic is sound (faster membrane damage, druggable target in solution), there is no experimental evidence that the pre-assembly mechanism actually provides an advantage in vivo, nor any demonstration of inhibitor molecules. These are reasonable hypotheses for future work but are not supported by data in this study.

result: Background claims about C. albicans pathogenesis and the role of candidalysin. These include statements about C. albicans as a serious fungal pathogen, its role in invasive candidiasis, the discovery and function of candidalysin as a virulence factor, and the rationale for studying its mechanism of action.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C15-C30 are background statements supported by established literature (multiple citations to Brown et al., Kullberg and Arendrup, Moyes et al., Naglik et al., Richardson et al., Kasper et al., Liu et al.). These provide appropriate context for the study and are well-documented in the literature. The logical inference about drug development (C29-C30) is reasonable.

result: Speculative mechanistic proposals about detergent effects on loop formation and the role of tryptophan at the N-terminus in impairing oligomer binding.
evaluation: Claims C78 and C103 are acknowledged as speculative by the authors. C78 suggests detergent might reduce loop formation based on limited data. C103 proposes a mechanism for G4W loss of function but lacks direct evidence (e.g., binding assays, structural data). These are reasonable hypotheses but require experimental validation.

result: Rationale for the G4W mutation based on the 8-mer model predicting a kink at G4 and the known flexibility conferred by glycine residues in α-helices.
evaluation: Claims C87-C89 provide the structural rationale for testing the G4W mutation. The model prediction of a kink at G4 (C88) is shown in Figure 6A, and the role of glycine in helix flexibility (C89) is supported by citation to Choy et al., 2003. This represents sound experimental design based on structural modeling.

result: Background on typical pore-forming toxin mechanisms, stating that PFTs are usually released as monomers that bind membranes and then oligomerize, often forming pre-pores before mature pores.
evaluation: Claims C111-C112 accurately describe established PFT mechanisms based on multiple citations (Leung et al., Verma et al., Mondal and Chattopadhyay, De Schutter et al.). This provides appropriate context for highlighting the novelty of the CL mechanism.
